source_read: Publisher HTML (onlinelibrary.wiley.com, Addiction 117(3), 532-544, 2022; first published 2 November 2021; open access), reached through https://doi.org/10.1111/add.15734 in my own browser tab: the full article page (abstract, Introduction, Methods, Results with Tables 1 and 2 as text, Discussion, Conclusions, declaration of interests, acknowledgements, author contributions); entries 22-52 of the reference list read with a page script to identify the cited studies. Not read: Figures 1 and 2 (images), the supporting information (Appendices A-C, Tables S1-S3), the PROSPERO record.

claims.note: The magnitude's figures match: 43% of 125 people who inject drugs changed behaviour, more likely when fentanyl was detected, aOR 5.08 (2.12-12.17), US, 2017. Ref. 22 is Peiper et al. 2019, titled as findings from a syringe services program in the southeastern United States, so 'at a US syringe services programme' is right. The review includes the Rhode Island study (refs. 31 and 34: Goldman 2019, Krieger 2018) and the Vancouver study (ref. 41), as the claim says. Its counts support 'mostly intentions and self-reports': 22 studies measured intended behaviour and 16 enacted behaviour, observed or self-reported from recall, 7 of them in both. On the claim's population clause '(or, in one study, their urine)': the review excluded studies that analysed human biological specimens; if the urine study is Peiper 2019, the review's text does not say what its participants tested, so this cannot be checked here.

anchors.locator: Results › Influence of DCS on behaviour of PWUD, 3rd paragraph
anchors.extracted: US cross-sectional study of people who inject drugs (n = 125, 2017; ref. 22): 43% changed their behaviour, more likely when fentanyl was detected, aOR 5.08 (95% CI 2.12-12.17); qualitative and longitudinal studies of young people who use drugs (n = 81, US, 2017; refs. 31, 34): fentanyl detection associated with using less, using with others and a test shot; self-reported behaviour more likely to change when fentanyl was detected.

anchors.locator: Results › Influence of DCS on behaviour of PWUD, 4th paragraph
anchors.extracted: Vancouver supervised injection site (n = 1411, 2016-17; ref. 41): intention to use a smaller quantity more likely when fentanyl was detected, OR 9.36 (4.25-20.65).

anchors.locator: Results › Influence of DCS on behaviour of PWUD, 5th paragraph
anchors.extracted: Disposal after fentanyl detection: 10% of young people who use drugs (n = 81; ref. 34); 0% of people who inject drugs (n = 125; ref. 22); qualitative work in Canada (n = 20): people using opioids less likely than people using stimulants to intend disposal if fentanyl was detected.

anchors.locator: Results › Influence of DCS on behaviour of PWUD, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: Enacted behaviour (observed or self-reported recall) measured in 16 studies (17.8%; refs. 22-37); intended behaviour in response to actual or hypothetical results in 22 (24.4%; refs. 31-52).

anchors.locator: Discussion, 3rd paragraph; Results › Study quality
anchors.extracted: Key limitations of the behaviour studies: cross-sectional designs and intention measures subject to the intention-behaviour gap; appraised studies not of high quality (11 cross-sectional articles scored 3 to 7 of 14); possible publication bias against studies without positive impacts.

anchors.locator: Reference list, refs. 22, 31, 34, 41
anchors.extracted: Ref. 22 Peiper et al. 2019 (fentanyl test strips at a syringe services program, southeastern US); ref. 31 Goldman et al. 2019; ref. 34 Krieger et al. 2018; ref. 41 Karamouzian et al. 2018.

claims.note: The review (to October 2019) neither measured nor discussed harms such as false reassurance; it reports only one study linking intentions with health outcomes, without a group lacking access, consistent with 'no study read compared people given kits with people not given them'. One relayed datum bears on the complacency critique, in the opposite direction: in a 2002 three-city European study, more frequent use of drug checking went with less frequent ecstasy use and less unsafe party behaviour (correlational, self-reported, a book the review did not appraise). The review also flags possible publication bias against studies without positive impacts. Its scope excludes people who obtained testing methods on their own rather than through a service; strips handed out by a service for personal use were included.

anchors.locator: Results › Influence of DCS on behaviour of PWUD, 4th paragraph
anchors.extracted: Only one study linked intended behaviours to observed health outcomes among people accessing drug checking (ref. 41, Vancouver).

anchors.locator: Results › Influence of DCS on behaviour of PWUD, 8th paragraph
anchors.extracted: In the multi-country study (Austria, Netherlands, Germany, n = 702, 2002; ref. 51), frequency of accessing drug checking was negatively correlated with frequency of ecstasy use and unsafe party behaviour; in all three European studies clients reported more frequent ecstasy use than non-clients.

anchors.locator: Discussion, 3rd paragraph
anchors.extracted: Publication bias may under-represent studies not showing positive impacts; grey literature and qualitative studies not appraised; intention measures subject to the intention-behaviour gap.

anchors.locator: Methods › Search strategy and selection criteria, 2nd paragraph
anchors.extracted: Excluded: analysis of human biological specimens; results not offered to clients; clients independently accessing analysis methods rather than a service; services not implemented.

claims.overstatement: 'Reports disposal from 0 to 10 in 100 across studies' reads as the range across the review's studies. The review lists eight studies with disposal as an outcome (observed: refs. 24, 26, 27, 32, 35; self-reported: 22, 31, 34) but prints a rate for only four: 0% (ref. 22), 4% (27), 7% (26) and 10% (34). Ref. 32 is Measham 2019, the English festival study that this same claim reports at 30 of 45 after a mis-sold result and 49 of 230 overall; the review's text gives it no rate (its supplementary tables were not read). Suggested wording: 'the rates it prints range from 0 to 10 in 100 (four of eight studies)'.
claims.note: Supported as printed: observed disposal at Canadian festivals 4% (cross-sectional, n = 2078, 2015; ref. 27, Sage 2016) and 7% (case report, n = 2786, 2014; ref. 26, Munn 2016), matching the magnitude; disposal more frequent after unexpected results (refs. 24, 27, 32, 52); search to 26 July 2018 with a full update on 16 October 2019, so 'to 2019' is right. The review also relays 0% disposal among 125 people who inject drugs at a US syringe services programme and, from qualitative work (n = 20), that people using opioids were less likely than people using stimulants to intend disposal after fentanyl detection, both consistent with 'few' among people who use opioids.

anchors.locator: Results › Influence of DCS on behaviour of PWUD, 5th paragraph
anchors.extracted: Disposal observed in 5 studies (refs. 24, 26, 27, 32, 35) and self-reported in 3 (22, 31, 34); more frequent when results were unexpected (24, 27, 32, 52); observed disposal among people at Canadian festivals 4% (n = 2078, 2015; ref. 27) to 7% (n = 2786, 2014; ref. 26); 10% of young people in the US when fentanyl was detected (n = 81; ref. 34); 0% of people who inject drugs (n = 125; ref. 22).

anchors.locator: Methods › Search strategy and selection criteria, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: Databases searched from 1 January 1990 to 26 July 2018, with a full update on 16 October 2019.

anchors.locator: Reference list, refs. 26, 27, 32
anchors.extracted: Ref. 26 Munn et al. 2016 (5-day electronic dance music event); ref. 27 Sage 2016 (Shambhala festival, ANKORS data 2015); ref. 32 Measham 2019 (the UK's first on-site drug checking service, English festival). The review prints no disposal rate for ref. 32.

claims.note: The review says only one study linked intended behaviours to observed health outcomes, and describes no other study with overdose outcomes, so 'found no other study linking testing with overdose' is a fair paraphrase. It relays that study's OR 0.41 as a link from intending to use less to fewer overdoses without the post-consumption caveat, and calls the 1411 checks people who inject drugs; elsewhere it notes that the Vancouver study reported mainly post-use access. The claim's reading (cannot show an effect) is the more accurate one.

anchors.locator: Results › Influence of DCS on behaviour of PWUD, 4th paragraph
anchors.extracted: Only one study (ref. 41, Vancouver supervised injection site, n = 1411, 2016-17) linked intended behaviours to observed health outcomes: those intending to use a smaller quantity were less likely to overdose, OR 0.41 (0.18-0.89), and to be given naloxone, OR 0.38 (0.15-0.96).

anchors.locator: Results › Influence of DCS on behaviour of PWUD, 8th paragraph
anchors.extracted: Among studies of people who inject drugs, the Canadian supervised-injection study (n = 1411) reported primarily post-use access, unlike two US studies with mainly pre-use access.

anchors.locator: Conclusions, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: Further research is needed on enacted behaviours, on linking behaviours to health outcomes, and among people who inject drugs or use opioids.

claims.overstatement: 'Than people at the same events who did not use the services' adds a detail the review does not give: it says only that the drug-use patterns of people in party settings who did and did not use drug checking were compared. Whether non-clients were sampled at the same events cannot be checked here. Suggested: 'than people in party settings who did not use the services'.
claims.note: Supported: in all three European book-length cross-sectional studies (Belgium n = 486, 2006; Netherlands n = 285, 2002; Austria, Netherlands and Germany n = 702, 2002; refs. 49-51: Houioux 2006, Korf 2003, Benschop 2002) clients reported more frequent ecstasy use than non-clients; self-reported. The same paragraph has qualifiers the claim could use: in the multi-country study more frequent use of drug checking went with less frequent ecstasy use and less unsafe party behaviour; in four studies 70% or more of people in party settings had not used drug-related services before; and 54% of the people who inject drugs in one US study were not syringe-programme clients. The three studies are books (grey literature) that the review did not appraise.

anchors.locator: Results › Influence of DCS on behaviour of PWUD, 8th paragraph
anchors.extracted: Drug-use patterns of people in party settings who did and did not use drug checking were compared in three European book-length cross-sectional studies (Belgium n = 486, 2006; Netherlands n = 285, 2002; Austria, Netherlands and Germany n = 702, 2002); in all three, clients reported higher frequencies of ecstasy use than non-clients.

anchors.locator: Results › Influence of DCS on behaviour of PWUD, 8th paragraph
anchors.extracted: Multi-country study: frequency of accessing drug checking negatively correlated with frequency of ecstasy use and unsafe party behaviour; 70% or more of people in party settings had not previously used drug-related services (4 studies); 54% of people who inject drugs in a US study (n = 125) were not existing syringe-programme clients.

anchors.locator: Methods › Screening, data extraction and quality assessment, 2nd paragraph; Discussion, 3rd paragraph
anchors.extracted: Risk of bias assessed only for peer-reviewed quantitative articles; grey literature (including books) not appraised.

anchors.locator: Reference list, refs. 49-51
anchors.extracted: Ref. 49 Houioux et al. 2006 (evaluation report, Belgium); ref. 50 Korf et al. 2003 (book, Netherlands); ref. 51 Benschop et al. 2002 (book, three European cities).

reporting_issues.note: The abstract's Methods does say risk of bias was assessed with NIH tools for quantitative peer-reviewed articles on behaviour or models; what the abstract omits is the result (all appraised studies of relatively poor quality). Suggested: 'The abstract mentions the appraisal but not its result'. The second half (the Discussion calls the market-monitoring evidence strong although appraisal was deemed inappropriate for those studies, Methods › Screening, data extraction and quality assessment, 2nd paragraph) is confirmed.

risk_of_bias.note: AMSTAR 2 critically low: items 7 and 9 unmet are enough; the other item judgments match the text.

interpretation_gap.note: Minor is defensible given the hedged abstract verb and the measured Conclusions; the Results' relay of the Vancouver OR 0.41 as a link to fewer overdoses is captured in reporting issue 3.

missed: Disposal 0-10%: analysis.effect_sizes ('Disposal 0% to 10% across studies'), interpretation_gap.results_show and the risk-of-bias reasoning ('for example disposal 0-10%') present the range as covering the studies; the review prints rates for 4 of its 8 disposal studies (refs. 22, 26, 27, 34), and ref. 32 (Measham 2019, the English festival) is among the eight without a printed rate. Qualify as 'the four rates printed in the text'.

comparison.controls says the three European book-length studies compared clients with 'people at the same events'; the review says only people in party settings who did and did not use drug checking (Results › Influence of DCS on behaviour of PWUD, 8th paragraph).

The 4% observed disposal (ref. 27) comes from the same Shambhala 2015 report (Sage 2016) that Karamouzian et al. 2018 relay as 13% after unexpected and 2% after expected results (sc_karamouzian_2018, Discussion, 2nd paragraph); the figures are compatible (overall against by result) and are one source, not two.
